decks.title: Cell Cycle and Cell Division — Part 1: The cell cycle and mitosis
goals: Describe the events of G1, S, G2 and M phases and the G0 stage; track the C-value and chromosome number through the cycle
Draw and label the stages of mitosis and state its significance in growth and repair
Work out phase durations, chromosome and chromatid counts, and a mitotic index from data

slides.heading: The cell cycle and mitosis
slides.body_md: Part 1: how a cell prepares to divide, and how mitosis shares the copied chromosomes equally.

visual.alt: Path from interphase through mitosis and cytokinesis to two daughter cells

slides.narration: A cell does not simply split. It first grows and copies its chromosomes in interphase, then divides its nucleus by mitosis and its cytoplasm by cytokinesis, producing two daughter cells.

slides.heading: Phases of the cell cycle
slides.body_md: The cycle has **interphase** (**G1, S, G2**) and the **M phase**. Cells that stop dividing leave G1 for **G0**.

slides.narration: In this culture the whole cycle takes twenty hours. Interphase is nearly all of it: nine hours in the first gap, seven hours for DNA synthesis, three and a half hours in the second gap. Mitosis takes only half an hour. Cells that stop dividing enter the resting state called G zero.

slides.heading: Events of each phase
slides.body_md: Each phase has its own job.

rows: Cell grows and makes RNA, proteins and organelles; prepares for DNA replication
DNA is replicated; each chromosome gets two chromatids; DNA amount doubles; chromosome number does not change; centrioles duplicate in animal cells
Growth continues; proteins for division, such as spindle proteins, are made; the copy is checked
Mitosis divides the nucleus; cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm
Quiescent: cells are alive and active but are not preparing to divide

visual.alt: Table of the events of the phases of the cell cycle

slides.narration: In the first gap the cell grows and builds what it needs. In S phase the DNA is copied. In the second gap the cell makes the proteins needed for division. Then mitosis and cytokinesis follow. Cells in the resting stage are active but not dividing.

slides.heading: C-value and chromosome number through the cycle
slides.body_md: The **C-value** is the amount of DNA in a haploid set. A cell in G1 has **2C**; after S phase it has **4C**; after division each daughter has **2C** again.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: phase times from a histogram
slides.body_md: A culture has a cycle of 20 hours. A flow-cytometry count of 2000 cells found 900 cells with 2C of DNA, 700 cells between 2C and 4C, and 400 cells with 4C. Find the time spent in each part of the cycle.
bullets: Time in a phase = (cells in that phase ÷ 2000) × 20 hours.
Cells with 4C are in G2 or in mitosis: 400 ÷ 2000 × 20 = 4 hours for G2 and M together.

slides.body_md: **Karyokinesis** (division of the nucleus) has four stages: **prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase**; **cytokinesis** divides the cytoplasm.

slides.narration: In prophase the chromosomes condense and the nuclear envelope breaks. In metaphase they line up on the equator. In anaphase the chromatids separate and move to opposite poles. In telophase two new nuclei form, and the cell then divides.

slides.heading: Events of mitosis
slides.body_md: Each stage has features that you should be able to draw.

rows: Chromatin condenses into chromosomes of two chromatids; centrosomes move apart and the spindle forms; nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear
Chromosomes line up on the equatorial plate; spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores; best stage to count chromosomes
Centromeres divide; chromatids separate and move to opposite poles
Chromosomes uncoil; nuclear envelope and nucleolus reappear
Animal cell: a furrow pinches the cell; plant cell: a cell plate grows from the centre

visual.alt: Table of the events of mitosis and cytokinesis

slides.narration: Prophase builds the chromosomes and spindle. Metaphase lines them up, and anaphase pulls the chromatids apart. Telophase reverses prophase by rebuilding the nuclei. An animal cell is then pinched by a furrow, while a plant cell builds a cell plate.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting chromosomes and chromatids
slides.body_md: A mouse-like cell has 40 chromosomes and 6.4 picograms of DNA in its G1 nucleus. Find the chromosomes, chromatids and DNA in the cell at G2, metaphase, anaphase and in each daughter nucleus.
bullets: After S phase: 40 chromosomes, each of two chromatids, so 80 chromatids; DNA = 2 × 6.4 = 12.8 picograms. The same holds at metaphase.
At anaphase the centromeres divide: each chromatid becomes a chromosome, so the whole cell has 80 chromosomes; DNA is still 12.8.
Each daughter nucleus gets 40 chromosomes (40 chromatids) and 6.4 picograms.

visual.alt: Worked table: chromosomes, chromatids and DNA through mitosis

slides.narration: S phase doubles the DNA and gives every chromosome two chromatids, but the number of chromosomes stays the same. At anaphase each chromatid counts as a chromosome, so the number doubles briefly. Each daughter cell receives the original number.

slides.heading: Quick check: metaphase
slides.body_md: In which stage of mitosis are the chromosomes arranged on the equatorial plate?
slides.narration: Quick check. In which stage are the chromosomes lined up on the equator?

slides.heading: Significance of mitosis
slides.body_md: Mitosis gives two daughter cells **genetically identical** to the parent cell.

rows: A zygote becomes a many-celled body; roots and shoots lengthen
Healing of a wound; replacement of skin and gut lining
Every body cell receives the full set of chromosomes
Unicellular organisms divide to form new individuals
Division restores the ratio of nucleus to cytoplasm

visual.alt: Table of the significance of mitosis

slides.narration: Mitosis lets a body grow and repair itself. Because each daughter receives an exact copy of every chromosome, all the cells of the body have the same genetic information. It is also how single-celled organisms reproduce.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the mitotic index
slides.body_md: In an onion root-tip squash, 600 cells were counted: 528 in interphase, 45 in prophase, 9 in metaphase, 6 in anaphase and 12 in telophase. The cell cycle takes 18 hours. Find the mitotic index and the time spent in prophase.
bullets: Dividing cells = 45 + 9 + 6 + 12 = 72. Mitotic index = 72 ÷ 600 × 100 = 12 percent.
Time in mitosis = 12 percent of 18 hours = 129.6 minutes.
Prophase: 45 ÷ 72 × 129.6 = 81 minutes, the longest stage because most dividing cells were in it.

visual.alt: Worked table: mitotic index 12 percent, prophase 81 minutes

slides.narration: The share of dividing cells is the mitotic index. The share of dividing cells found in a stage tells us the share of the time that the stage takes. Here prophase is the longest stage and anaphase the shortest.

slides.heading: Quick check: mitotic index
slides.body_md: What does a high mitotic index in a tissue show?
slides.narration: Quick check. What does a high mitotic index tell us?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Cell cycle: G1, S, G2 (interphase) and M; G0 is the resting state.
C-value: 2C in G1, 4C after S, 2C in each daughter; chromosome number unchanged in S phase.
Mitosis: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, then cytokinesis; daughters are identical to the parent.
Significance: growth, repair, constant chromosome number, asexual reproduction.

visual.alt: Summary table of key points

slides.narration: To recap: interphase prepares the cell, S phase copies the DNA, mitosis shares it equally and cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm. The daughter cells are identical to the parent.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Draw **metaphase** and **anaphase** with spindle fibres and labelled chromosomes.
Track **C-value, chromosomes and chromatids** at each stage.
Say that **S phase doubles DNA but not the chromosome number**.
Give **growth and repair** as the significance of mitosis.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Draw metaphase and anaphase with labels. Track the DNA amount, chromosomes and chromatids stage by stage. Remember that S phase doubles the DNA but not the chromosome number. And give growth and repair as the importance of mitosis.

slides.heading: Meiosis: halving the chromosome number
slides.body_md: Part 2: the special division that makes gametes, and how it differs from mitosis.

visual.alt: Path from a diploid parent cell through meiosis I and II to four haploid cells

slides.narration: Sexual reproduction needs cells with half the usual number of chromosomes. Meiosis achieves this with two divisions after a single copying of the DNA, so one parent cell gives four cells with half the number.

slides.heading: Overview of meiosis

slides.narration: In leptotene the chromosomes appear as thin threads. In zygotene the homologous chromosomes pair, which is called synapsis. In pachytene crossing over takes place. In diplotene the homologues start to separate but stay joined at chiasmata. In diakinesis the chromosomes are most condensed.

slides.heading: Events of the substages
slides.body_md: Synapsis and crossing over are the key events of prophase I.

rows: Chromosomes become visible as long, thin threads
**Synapsis**: homologous chromosomes pair, forming **bivalents** with a synaptonemal complex
Chromosomes thicken; **crossing over** exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids at recombination nodules
Synaptonemal complex dissolves; homologues separate but stay joined at **chiasmata**
Chiasmata move to the ends (terminalisation); chromosomes fully condensed; nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear

visual.alt: Table of the five substages of prophase I

slides.narration: Pairing in zygotene makes bivalents. Crossing over in pachytene swaps segments of non-sister chromatids. The crossing points show as chiasmata in diplotene, and in diakinesis the chromosomes are fully condensed and ready for the spindle.

slides.heading: Quick check: synapsis
slides.body_md: In which substage of prophase I does synapsis take place?
slides.narration: Quick check. In which substage do homologous chromosomes pair?

slides.heading: The rest of meiosis
slides.body_md: After prophase I the stages resemble those of mitosis, but with important differences.

rows: Bivalents line up on the equator; the kinetochores of homologues face opposite poles
Homologous chromosomes separate and move to the poles; centromeres do not divide
Two cells (a dyad), each with half the chromosome number
Prophase II, metaphase II, anaphase II (centromeres divide; chromatids separate) and telophase II give four haploid cells (a tetrad)

visual.alt: Table of metaphase I to the end of meiosis II

slides.narration: In anaphase one, whole chromosomes move apart, so each daughter cell gets one member of each pair. There is no DNA copying between the divisions. In the second division the chromatids separate, as in mitosis, giving four cells.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: DNA and chromosomes through meiosis
slides.body_md: A mouse-like cell has 40 chromosomes and 6.4 picograms of DNA in G1. Track chromosomes, chromatids and DNA in the cell through meiosis.
bullets: After S phase: 40 chromosomes, 80 chromatids and 12.8 picograms. This holds through prophase I and metaphase I.
Meiosis I halves the chromosome number: each of the two cells has 20 chromosomes of two chromatids, with 6.4 picograms.
Meiosis II separates the chromatids: each of the four cells has 20 chromosomes of one chromatid, with 3.2 picograms, half the amount in G1.

visual.alt: Worked table: chromosomes, chromatids and DNA through meiosis

slides.narration: The number of chromosomes halves at the end of the first division, but each chromosome still has two chromatids. The DNA amount per cell falls to the G one value then. It halves again after the second division, so a gamete has half the DNA of a G one cell.

slides.heading: Significance of meiosis: variation
slides.body_md: Meiosis keeps the chromosome number constant from generation to generation and creates **genetic variation**.

rows: Exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids gives new combinations of genes on a chromosome
Each bivalent lines up at random at metaphase I, so maternal and paternal chromosomes are shuffled
Random fusion of two different gametes
Halving at meiosis balances the doubling at fertilisation

visual.alt: Table of the sources of variation in meiosis

slides.narration: Crossing over mixes genes within a chromosome. The random lining up of the pairs mixes whole chromosomes. Random fertilisation adds further variety. Meiosis also stops the chromosome number from doubling every generation.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how many kinds of gamete?
slides.body_md: A lily has 24 chromosomes in its body cells. Ignoring crossing over, how many different chromosome combinations can its gametes have, and how many for the zygotes from two such parents?
bullets: Bivalents = 24 ÷ 2 = 12. Each bivalent can face either pole at anaphase I.
Gamete types = 2 multiplied by itself 12 times = 4096.
Zygote combinations = 4096 × 4096 = 16777216. Crossing over increases the variety still further.

visual.alt: Worked table: 4096 gamete types

slides.narration: Each pair of chromosomes can line up in either direction, so with twelve pairs there are two to the power twelve possible gametes. The combinations in the zygote are the square of that number. Crossing over adds even more variety.

slides.heading: Quick check: anaphase I
slides.body_md: What separates at anaphase I of meiosis?
slides.narration: Quick check. What moves to the poles in anaphase one?

slides.heading: Mitosis and meiosis compared
slides.body_md: The two divisions differ in where, how often and how they divide.

rows: Body cells and cells that divide to grow
Gamete mother cells in the reproductive organs
Four, different from each other and the parent
Synapsis in zygotene; crossing over in pachytene

visual.alt: Table of the differences between mitosis and meiosis

slides.narration: Mitosis is a single division that copies a cell exactly. Meiosis is two divisions that halve the number and shuffle the genes. Only meiosis involves pairing of homologues and crossing over, and only meiosis makes cells that differ from each other.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: counting sperm and recombinants
slides.body_md: A male needs to make 600 sperm. (a) How many primary spermatocytes must divide, and how many secondary spermatocytes form? (b) In 500 gametes from meioses in which 40 percent had one crossover between two genes, how many gametes are recombinant?
bullets: (a) One primary spermatocyte gives four sperm: 600 ÷ 4 = 150 primary spermatocytes; each makes two secondary spermatocytes: 300.
(b) A meiosis with one crossover gives two parental and two recombinant gametes, so half of its gametes are recombinant: 0.4 × ½ × 500 = 100.

visual.alt: Worked table: spermatocyte and recombinant counts

slides.narration: Each primary cell gives four sperm, so divide the number of sperm by four. For recombinants, a crossover makes half of the gametes of that meiosis recombinant, so multiply the share of meioses with a crossover by one half.

slides.heading: Quick check: comparison
slides.body_md: How many daughter cells does one meiotic division sequence produce, and with what chromosome number?
slides.narration: Quick check. How many cells does meiosis produce, and how do they compare with the parent?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Meiosis: two divisions after one S phase; meiosis I separates homologues, meiosis II separates chromatids; four haploid cells.
Prophase I: leptotene, zygotene (synapsis), pachytene (crossing over), diplotene (chiasmata), diakinesis.
Variation: crossing over, independent assortment and fertilisation.
Mitosis: one division, two identical cells, same number; meiosis: two divisions, four different cells, half the number.

visual.alt: Summary table of key points

slides.narration: To recap: meiosis halves the chromosome number in its first division and separates chromatids in its second. Prophase one has five substages with synapsis and crossing over, and the result is variation.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name the **five substages** of prophase I in order, with the key event of each.
State that **synapsis** is pairing and **crossing over** is exchange between non-sister chromatids.
Explain **how meiosis produces variation**.
Tabulate **mitosis against meiosis** with at least five points.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Name the five substages of prophase one in order. Define synapsis and crossing over. Explain how meiosis gives variation. And compare mitosis with meiosis in a table of at least five points.

sections.heading: 1. The cell cycle: G1, S, G2, M and G0; C-value
sections.body_md:
The **cell cycle** is the sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its contents and divides. It has two parts: **interphase** and the **M phase** (mitosis and cytokinesis). Interphase is the longest part (in the model culture 19.5 of 20 hours, 97.5 percent) and has three phases:
- **G1 (first gap):** the cell grows and makes RNA, proteins and organelles; it prepares for DNA replication.
- **S (synthesis):** the **DNA is replicated**; every chromosome now has two chromatids. The DNA content doubles (**2C to 4C**) but the **number of chromosomes does not change**. In animal cells the centrioles also duplicate.
- **G2 (second gap):** growth continues; proteins needed for division, such as those of the spindle, are made.

**M phase:** nuclear division (**karyokinesis**) and division of the cytoplasm (**cytokinesis**); it is the shortest phase (about one hour in a human cell with a 24-hour cycle; 0.5 hour here).

**G0 (quiescent stage):** cells that do not divide further, or divide only when needed, leave the cycle from G1; they are alive and metabolically active (for example adult heart and nerve cells).

**C-value** is the amount of DNA in the haploid set of chromosomes. A diploid cell in G1 has **2C**, after S phase **4C**, and each daughter after mitosis **2C** again; a gamete has **1C**. In the mouse-like example of 40 chromosomes, the DNA in a G1 nucleus is 6.4 picograms and 12.8 picograms in G2; the chromosome number is 40 in both, but the chromatids rise from 40 to 80.

key_terms.definition_md: G1, S and G2 together: the period between divisions.
Amount of DNA in a haploid set; a G1 diploid cell is 2C.
Resting state in which a cell has left the cell cycle.

sections.heading: 2. Mitosis
sections.body_md:
**Mitosis** is the **equational division** in which a parent cell gives two daughter cells with the same chromosome number and the same genetic content.

- **Prophase:** chromatin condenses into chromosomes, each of two chromatids joined at the centromere; the centrosomes move to opposite poles and the **spindle** forms; the **nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear**.
- **Metaphase:** the chromosomes line up on the **equatorial (metaphase) plate**, with spindle fibres attached to the **kinetochores** at the centromeres; the best stage for counting and studying chromosomes.
- **Anaphase:** the **centromeres divide**; each chromatid is now a chromosome and the two sets move to opposite poles (so the whole cell briefly has 80 chromosomes in the 40-chromosome example).
- **Telophase:** chromosomes uncoil into chromatin; the **nuclear envelope and nucleolus reappear**, giving two nuclei.
- **Cytokinesis:** in an **animal cell** a **furrow** pinches the cell in two; in a **plant cell** a **cell plate** grows outwards from the centre to the wall.

**Significance:** growth of the body, repair and replacement of cells, constant chromosome number in all body cells, asexual reproduction of unicellular organisms, and the restoration of the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio.

**Mitotic index** = dividing cells ÷ cells counted × 100. In the onion root-tip squash of 600 cells it is 12 percent.

key_terms.definition_md: Nuclear division giving two genetically identical nuclei.
Protein disc on the centromere where spindle fibres attach.
Structure that forms the new wall between daughter plant cells.

sections.heading: 3. Meiosis
sections.body_md:
**Meiosis** occurs in the gamete mother cells and consists of **two successive divisions** (meiosis I and II) after a single DNA replication, producing **four haploid cells**. **Meiosis I is the reductional division; meiosis II is equational.**

**Prophase I** is long and has five substages:
1. **Leptotene** — chromosomes appear as long, thin threads.
2. **Zygotene** — **synapsis**: homologous chromosomes pair (a synaptonemal complex forms), making **bivalents**.
3. **Pachytene** — chromosomes thicken; **crossing over** exchanges segments between **non-sister chromatids** of homologues at recombination nodules (a tetrad of four chromatids is visible).
4. **Diplotene** — the synaptonemal complex dissolves; homologues begin to separate but remain joined at **chiasmata**, the sites of crossing over.
5. **Diakinesis** — **terminalisation** of chiasmata; chromosomes fully condensed; nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear; the spindle forms.

**Metaphase I:** bivalents lie on the equator, the kinetochores of the two homologues facing opposite poles. **Anaphase I:** homologous chromosomes separate (centromeres do not divide). **Telophase I:** two cells (a **dyad**), each with half the chromosome number. **Interkinesis** is a short pause with **no DNA replication**. **Meiosis II** (prophase II to telophase II) separates the **sister chromatids**, giving **four haploid cells (a tetrad)**.

**Significance:** keeps the chromosome number constant from generation to generation; produces **variation** through **crossing over**, **independent assortment** (a lily with 24 chromosomes can make 4096 chromosome combinations in gametes, ignoring crossing over) and random fertilisation, which drives evolution. In the 40-chromosome example the DNA falls from 12.8 picograms (after S) to 6.4 after meiosis I and 3.2 in each gamete.

sections.heading: 4. Differences between mitosis and meiosis
sections.body_md:
| Feature | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Where | Body cells; cells that divide for growth | Gamete mother cells in the reproductive organs |
| Divisions | One | Two |
| Daughter cells | Two, identical to the parent | Four, genetically different |
| Chromosome number | Same as the parent (2n) | Halved (n) |
| Synapsis and crossing over | Absent | Present (zygotene and pachytene) |
| Prophase | Short, without substages | Long, with five substages |
| Metaphase plate | Individual chromosomes | Bivalents (metaphase I) |
| Anaphase | Chromatids separate | Homologues separate (I), chromatids separate (II) |
| Role | Growth, repair, asexual reproduction | Gamete formation and variation |

**Similarity:** both are preceded by DNA replication in the S phase and both use a spindle to move chromosomes.

Mitosis and meiosis II, in which the number is unchanged.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying that the chromosome number doubles in S phase (the DNA amount and chromatid number double, not the chromosomes).
- Saying that the centromere divides at anaphase I (it divides at anaphase II and at anaphase of mitosis).
- Placing crossing over in zygotene (it is in pachytene; pairing is in zygotene).
- Writing that meiosis II halves the chromosome number (meiosis I does; meiosis II is equational).
- Giving a cell plate for an animal cell (a furrow) or a furrow for a plant cell (a cell plate).
- Writing that interkinesis includes DNA replication (it does not).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a phase or stage, a term (synapsis, chiasma), a number (chromosomes, chromatids), give-a-reason and analogy.
- 2–3-mark questions: events of a phase; the stages of prophase I; significance of mitosis or meiosis; differences in a table.
- 5-mark questions in parts: labelled diagrams of the stages of mitosis; prophase I with diagrams; mitosis against meiosis.

questions.stem_md: Name the three phases of interphase and state one main event in each.

answer.model_answer_md: **G1**: the cell grows and makes proteins and organelles. **S**: the **DNA is replicated**, so every chromosome has two chromatids. **G2**: growth continues and proteins needed for division, such as those of the spindle, are made.

questions.stem_md: A diploid cell has 2C of DNA in G1. State its C-value after S phase and in each daughter cell after mitosis, and say what happens to the chromosome number in S phase.

answer.model_answer_md: After S phase the cell has **4C**; each daughter cell after mitosis has **2C** again. In S phase the **chromosome number does not change**, because the DNA is copied into chromatids that remain attached.

questions.stem_md: What is the G0 stage? State two features of a cell in it.

answer.model_answer_md: G0 is the **quiescent stage**, in which a cell has **left the cell cycle** after G1. The cell is **alive and metabolically active** but **does not divide** (it may re-enter the cycle when stimulated).

questions.stem_md: A student says that “everything doubles in S phase”. State what does double, what does not, and why the cell still has the same number of chromosomes.

answer.model_answer_md: In S phase the **DNA content doubles** (2C to 4C) and the **number of chromatids doubles**, because each chromosome is replicated. The **number of chromosomes does not double**, since the two identical chromatids of each chromosome remain joined at the **centromere** and are counted as one chromosome. So the student’s statement is wrong for the chromosome number.

questions.solution_md: DNA and chromatids double; chromosomes do not.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the phases of the cell cycle and state one event of each phase of interphase. [2]
(b) Describe how the DNA content (C-value) of a diploid cell changes through one cycle, from G1 to the two daughter cells. [2]
(c) What is meant by G0? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The cycle has **G1, S, G2** (interphase) and **M** (mitosis and cytokinesis). **G1**: growth and synthesis of proteins; **S**: DNA replication; **G2**: preparation for division.

(b) A G1 cell has **2C**; the DNA is replicated in S phase so it rises to **4C**, which stays through G2 and mitosis until the cell divides; each daughter cell then has **2C** again. The chromosome number does not change in S phase.

(c) **G0** is the **resting stage** into which a cell may leave the cell cycle from G1; the cell is alive but not dividing.

options.text_md: It is in G1: the DNA has not been replicated.
It is in prophase: the nucleolus and nuclear envelope have disappeared.
It is in anaphase: the chromatids have separated.
It is in telophase: the envelope has re-formed.

questions.solution_md: Condensed double chromosomes with no envelope mean prophase (late) — option (b).

options.text_md: The chromosomes uncoil and the nuclear envelope and nucleolus reappear
The chromosomes condense and the nucleolus disappears
The chromosomes line up on the equator

questions.solution_md: Telophase reverses the changes of prophase — option (a).

questions.solution_md: Mitosis gives each daughter nucleus the full set — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The two daughter cells formed by mitosis are genetically identical to the parent cell.

**Reason (R):** The chromatids that separate at anaphase are exact copies made in the S phase.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the identical chromatids explain the identical daughters — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Metaphase is the best stage for counting the chromosomes of a cell.

answer.model_answer_md: The chromosomes are **fully condensed** and lie **in one plane on the equator**, so they are easy to see and count.

questions.solution_md: Condensed and in one plane.

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy: Animal cell : furrow :: Plant cell : ______

answer.model_answer_md: **Cell plate**.

questions.solution_md: Cell plate.

questions.stem_md: A mouse-like cell has 40 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does the whole cell contain at anaphase of mitosis, counting each separated chromatid as a chromosome?
questions.solution_md: 40 chromosomes of two chromatids give $2 \times 40 = 80$ separated chromatids, each a chromosome.

questions.stem_md: In a squash of 250 root-tip cells, 40 are found in some stage of mitosis. Calculate the mitotic index as a percentage.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{40}{250} \times 100 = 16$ percent.

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which mitosis is important to a plant and one way in which it is important to a unicellular organism.

answer.model_answer_md: In a plant mitosis allows **growth** (for example lengthening of roots and shoots) and **repair or replacement** of damaged cells, and it keeps the **chromosome number** the same in all cells. In a unicellular organism mitosis is the means of **asexual reproduction**.

questions.solution_md: Two plant roles; one unicellular role.

questions.stem_md: Describe what happens to the chromosomes and to the spindle fibres at metaphase and at anaphase of mitosis.

answer.model_answer_md: At **metaphase** the chromosomes line up on the **equatorial plate**, each attached by its **kinetochores** to spindle fibres from **opposite poles**. At **anaphase** the **centromeres divide**, so the two chromatids of each chromosome separate, and the fibres **shorten** and pull the chromatids, now chromosomes, to **opposite poles**.

questions.solution_md: Alignment; centromere division; movement.

marking_scheme.step: Chromosomes on the equator, fibres attached

questions.stem_md: A burn on the skin heals within a few weeks. Explain which kind of cell division is responsible, why the new cells are suitable replacements, and what makes the daughter cells identical.

answer.model_answer_md: **Mitosis** of the cells at the edge of the wound makes new cells. They are suitable replacements because each daughter cell receives the **same number of chromosomes and the same genes** as the parent. This is because the DNA is **replicated in S phase** and the **chromatids separate equally at anaphase**.

questions.solution_md: Mitosis; identical; replication and separation.

questions.stem_md: A lily cell has 24 chromosomes. Give the number of chromosomes and of chromatids in the cell at G1, at metaphase and in each daughter nucleus after mitosis.

answer.model_answer_md: At **G1** the cell has **24 chromosomes** and **24 chromatids** (one each). At **metaphase** it has **24 chromosomes** and **48 chromatids**. Each **daughter nucleus** has **24 chromosomes** and **24 chromatids**.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw labelled diagrams of metaphase and anaphase in an animal cell with four chromosomes. [2]
(b) State what happens to the centromeres and chromatids at anaphase. [1]
(c) State two ways in which mitosis is significant to a many-celled organism. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Metaphase diagram:** four chromosomes, each of two chromatids, on the **equatorial plate**, with **spindle fibres** from the two **centrosomes** attached to the **kinetochores**. **Anaphase diagram:** two groups of four chromatids (now chromosomes), V-shaped with the **centromeres leading**, moving towards opposite **poles**.

(b) The **centromeres divide**, the **sister chromatids separate**, and each moves to an opposite pole.

(c) Mitosis allows **growth** of the body and **repair or replacement** of cells; it also keeps the **chromosome number constant** in every body cell.

questions.solution_md: Diagrams; centromere division; significance.

questions.solution_md: A shows four thick paired chromatids with a recombination nodule: pachytene — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Define synapsis and name the substage of prophase I in which it occurs.

answer.model_answer_md: **Synapsis** is the **pairing of homologous chromosomes** along their length to form **bivalents**, held by a synaptonemal complex. It occurs in the **zygotene** substage of prophase I.

questions.solution_md: Pairing of homologues; zygotene.

questions.stem_md: What is crossing over? Name the chromatids involved and the substage in which it takes place.

answer.model_answer_md: **Crossing over** is the **exchange of segments** between **non-sister chromatids** of homologous chromosomes. It takes place in the **pachytene** substage of prophase I and produces new combinations of genes.

questions.solution_md: Exchange; non-sister chromatids; pachytene.

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which meiosis II resembles mitosis, and name the cells it produces.

answer.model_answer_md: In meiosis II, as in mitosis, the **centromeres divide** and **sister chromatids separate**, and the **chromosome number does not change**. It produces **four haploid cells**, called a **tetrad**, from the two cells of the dyad.

questions.solution_md: Two likenesses; four haploid cells.

questions.stem_md: What is interkinesis? State two features of it.

answer.model_answer_md: **Interkinesis** is the **short pause between meiosis I and meiosis II**. It has **no DNA replication**, and the chromosomes may uncoil slightly while the two cells of the dyad prepare for the second division.

questions.solution_md: Pause; no DNA replication.

questions.stem_md: Describe what happens to the chromosomes in leptotene, zygotene and pachytene of prophase I.

answer.model_answer_md: In **leptotene** the chromosomes appear as long, **thin threads**. In **zygotene** the homologous chromosomes **pair (synapsis)** to form bivalents. In **pachytene** the chromosomes become **thick**, each bivalent shows four chromatids, and **crossing over** takes place between non-sister chromatids at recombination nodules. These three substages come before diplotene and diakinesis, when the chromosomes separate and condense fully.

questions.solution_md: Three substages.

questions.stem_md: Describe diplotene and diakinesis, and name the structure that shows where crossing over took place.

answer.model_answer_md: In **diplotene** the synaptonemal complex dissolves and the homologues begin to **separate**, but they stay joined at **chiasmata**, which show where crossing over took place. In **diakinesis** the chiasmata move to the ends (**terminalisation**), the chromosomes are **fully condensed**, and the **nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear**.

questions.solution_md: Diplotene, chiasmata; diakinesis.

questions.stem_md: Explain two ways in which meiosis produces genetic variation among gametes, and say what fertilisation adds.

answer.model_answer_md: **Crossing over** in pachytene exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids, giving **new combinations of genes**. **Independent assortment** at metaphase I lets each bivalent line up at random, so the **maternal and paternal chromosomes are shuffled** into the gametes. **Fertilisation** adds more variety because any male gamete may fuse with any female gamete.

questions.solution_md: Crossing over; assortment; fertilisation.

questions.stem_md: Explain, using chromosome numbers, why the chromosome number of a species stays constant from generation to generation although two gametes fuse at fertilisation.

answer.model_answer_md: Each gamete is **haploid (n)** because meiosis **halves** the chromosome number of the gamete mother cell. At fertilisation, two haploid gametes fuse to form a **diploid zygote (2n)**. If gametes were formed by mitosis they would be 2n and the number would **double in every generation**, but meiosis **restores balance**.

questions.solution_md: Halving at meiosis balances doubling at fertilisation.

answer.model_answer_md: At the end of **meiosis I** there are **two** cells (secondary spermatocytes), each with **20 chromosomes**, each of two chromatids. At the end of **meiosis II** there are **four** cells (spermatids), each with **20 chromosomes**, each of a single chromatid.

In **diplotene** the synaptonemal complex dissolves and the homologues begin to separate but remain joined at **chiasmata**.

questions.stem_md:

(c) Explain how meiosis produces genetic variation. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) At **anaphase I** the **homologous chromosomes** separate; at **anaphase II** the **sister chromatids** separate.

(b) A cell with **six chromosomes** replicates its DNA once, then divides **twice**. (c) **Crossing over** gives new gene combinations on chromosomes, and **independent assortment** of the bivalents at metaphase I shuffles maternal and paternal chromosomes; random fertilisation adds more.

questions.solution_md: Separation; halving; variation.

**Either** (i): Explain why the spermatid has half the DNA of the spermatogonium in G1.

answer.model_answer_md: The spermatid is **haploid**: the DNA was replicated once but the cell divided **twice**, and meiosis II **separated the sister chromatids**, so each cell received **one chromatid** of each chromosome.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): The spermatid is later changed into a sperm. State the DNA in a sperm and in the zygote formed with an egg of the same species.

answer.model_answer_md: The sperm has **3.2 picograms** (haploid). The zygote receives the same amount from the egg, so it has **6.4 picograms**, the diploid G1 amount of 6.4.
